# Data

The MOSAIC model requires a diverse set of data sources, some of which are directly used to define model parameters (e.g., birth and death rates), while others help fit models a priori and provide informative priors for the transmission model. As additional data sources become available, future versions of the model will adapt to incorporate them. For now, the following data sources represent the minimum requirements to initiate a viable first model.

## Historical Incidence and Deaths

Data on historical cholera incidence and deaths are crucial for establishing baseline transmission patterns. We compiled the annual total reported cases and deaths for all AFRO region countries from January 1970 through the most recent complete calendar year (2025) plus a partial-year snapshot for the current year. These data comes from several sources which include:


1. **Our World in Data (1970-2021)**: [Number of Reported Cases of Cholera (1949-2021)](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-reported-cases-of-cholera) and the [Number of Reported Deaths of Cholera from (1949-2021)](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-reported-cholera-deaths). The Our World in Data group compiled these data from previously published annual WHO reports.
2. **WHO Annual Report 2022**: These data were manually extracted from the World Health Organization's [Weekly Epidemiological Record](https://www.who.int/publications/journals/weekly-epidemiological-record) No 38, 2023, 98, 431–452.
3. **Global Cholera and Acute Watery Diarrhea Dashboard (2023+)**: Year-filtered CSVs for 2023, 2024, 2025, and rolling snapshots of the current year are available at the [WHO Global Cholera and AWD Dashboard](https://who-global-cholera-and-awd-dashboard-1-who.hub.arcgis.com/). Each row's actual year is derived from its `first_epiwk` / `last_epiwk` range, and partial-year coverage is tracked explicitly via `coverage_days` / `year_fraction` columns so partial snapshots can be ingested alongside full-year totals without mislabeling.

These annual totals are also the WHO account of each country-year against which imputed weekly counts are reconciled (see [Surveillance reconciliation](#surveillance-reconciliation) below).


## Recent Incidence and Deaths

To capture recent cholera trends, we retrieved reported cases and deaths data from the [WHO Global Cholera and Acute Watery Diarrhea Dashboard](https://who-global-cholera-and-awd-dashboard-1-who.hub.arcgis.com/) REST API. These data provide weekly incidence and deaths from January 2023 onward, with the current-year rolling snapshot updated on each pipeline run, providing up-to-date counts at the country level.

Note that WHO's epidemiological weeks are not ISO-8601 weeks. A WHO week runs from Monday to Sunday and is stamped with its Monday (the dashboard's note: "the date corresponds to the first day of the epi-week (from Monday to Sunday)"), but the weeks are numbered as on the MMWR (US CDC) calendar shifted by one day: week 1 begins on the Monday after the Sunday that starts MMWR week 1, the Sunday-to-Saturday week that contains 4 January. This coincides with ISO-8601 weeks except in years whose 4 January falls on a Sunday: WHO has a genuine week 53 of 2025, starting Monday 29 December 2025 (ISO 2025 has only 52 weeks), and WHO week 1 of 2026 starts on 5 January 2026. We therefore date every weekly row from WHO's own calendar (Monday to Sunday), keep a real week 53 as its own week rather than merging it into a neighbour, and key all downstream processing on the week's start date rather than on the (year, week) label. A missing case or death count stays missing; no row is dropped because one of its two fields is missing.

We also use the country-level weekly series of the Johns Hopkins public cholera surveillance dataset (compiled by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and retrieved with the `jhu_cholera_data` scraper, a private repository) as back-history before the WHO dashboard era. Cases are the suspected count when present, otherwise the confirmed count. A missing death count is kept as missing (`NA`), not recorded as zero: about three quarters of the country-level rows in the archive carry no death count, and treating them as observed zeros would bias the deaths likelihood and any case fatality estimate. Rows with neither a case nor a death count are dropped.

### Surveillance reconciliation

We assemble the weekly series that the model is calibrated to (`reported_cases` and `reported_deaths` in the model configuration) with `process_cholera_surveillance_data()`, from four sources: the WHO dashboard and the Johns Hopkins series described above, counts extracted from situation reports and other documents by the [ai-cholera-data-mining](https://github.com/InstituteforDiseaseModeling/ai-cholera-data-mining) pipeline (AI; `process_AI_cholera_data()`), and supplementary outbreak line lists (`process_SUPP_weekly_data()`). The sources overlap, report late or in batches, and sometimes repeat one another, so we reconcile each country-week before the weekly totals are spread over the days of their week. Every week that a rule below changes is listed, with its values before and after and the evidence, in the adjustment log `cholera_surveillance_weekly_adjustments.csv`, written beside the combined weekly file.

**Trust tiers.** Each weekly row is ranked by how its count was obtained: *observed* (a direct WHO, JHU or supplementary count, or an AI-extracted weekly count or documented zero), *reconstructed* (a WHO multi-week report spread over the weeks it covers, whose total is reported but whose timing within the window is not), or *imputed* (a multi-week or annual total spread over weeks by the AI pipeline's seasonal template, or any other modelled value). Where several sources report the same country-week, one whole row supplies it: a row with a count beats an empty one, observed beats reconstructed beats imputed whatever the source, a row with a case count beats a deaths-only row, and the source priority WHO > JHU > AI > supplementary decides the rest. Each week carries a confidence weight, 1 for a direct WHO, JHU or supplementary count and lower otherwise, which the likelihood applies to that week's score. Its tier reaches the model configuration as `reported_tier` (1 observed, 2 reconstructed, 3 imputed), so that the dispersions of the likelihood are estimated from observed weeks wherever a location has enough of them (see the [Negative Binomial density](https://www.mosaicmod.org/model-calibration-1.html#negative-binomial-density) on the Model Calibration page for the cases and the [Case fatality rate](https://www.mosaicmod.org/model-description.html#case-fatality-rate) on the Model Description page for the deaths).

**WHO multi-week reports.** The dashboard enters a zero both for a week with no cases and for a week with no report, and books a late or batched report in the week it arrives, so a backlog appears as a one-week spike that no transmission model can reproduce. We read a report as covering several weeks (`process_WHO_weekly_data()`) when it has at least 20 cases, follows a silent week (a reported zero or no report) of the same epidemiological year, and is followed by a fall that an epidemic curve cannot produce: it is at least twice each of the next four reported weeks, or the next two reported weeks are both zero. A report that passes only the first of these two tests may cover at most four reported zeros, unless at least two of the next four reported weeks are zero (batch reporting), so that an explosive outbreak onset after a long silence is not spread. The report is then spread evenly over the silent weeks back to the previous non-zero report, never before week 1 of its epidemiological year, in whole counts that leave every country-year total unchanged; weeks with no report at all are included only when the outbreak was over by the time it was reported (the next four reported weeks all zero). The spread weeks are reconstructed, with a confidence weight that falls with the length of the window (0.9 up to four weeks, 0.8 up to 13, 0.7 up to 26, otherwise 0.5), and the as-published counts are kept beside them.

**Curated windows.** Where a documented source dates the outbreak that a report covers, a curated table (`inst/extdata/surveillance_curation.csv` in MOSAIC-pkg, which gives the evidence and reference for every row) replaces the rule for that report. Namibia 2025 is spread from the week of its first case (Sunday 2 March, week 9); reports from Côte d'Ivoire 2025 and Nigeria 2023 that the rule would leave in place are spread over the weeks they cover; and South Africa 2023, whose first dashboard row (week 35: 1,390 cases, 47 deaths) carries the whole outbreak, is spread over 1 February to 31 July, the outbreak period in the Department of Health's statement of 5 July 2023 and the date of the count in WHO AFRO's [after-action review](https://www.afro.who.int/countries/south-africa/news/cholera-outbreak-response-and-after-action-review). Where documented dates also time the outbreak, the window is *shaped* rather than spread evenly: cumulative-count anchors (`inst/extdata/surveillance_curation_shapes.csv`) give a case curve and, optionally, a deaths curve (otherwise deaths follow the cases); each week receives the report's cases and deaths in proportion to the curve's increment over its Monday-to-Sunday span; and the curve's total must lie between half the report and 2% above it. South Africa 2023 follows WHO's epidemic curve of the outbreak ([Multi-country outbreak of cholera, external situation report #5](https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/multi-country-outbreak-of-cholera--external-situation-report--5---4-august-2023), Figure 5) with its symptom onset dates moved two days later to report dates, the lag at which the onset curve best matches the notification-date curve of situation report #4, so that the window is dated like the rest of the WHO weekly rows, which the model fits with a single reporting delay; the imported case of 14 July is placed by the same rule. A few sporadic cases from February to April precede the Hammanskraal surge, which peaks at 432 cases in the week of 22-28 May. Its deaths follow the national death counts reported by date, from the first death, announced on 23 February, to 47 deaths by 4 July. The totals are unchanged. Shaped weeks are labelled `who_catchup_curated_shaped` (reconstructed, confidence 0.9). Unlike the even spread, the shaped window gives the outbreak a peak that the epidemic-peak detector (below) finds.

**Cross-source double counting.** Inside a WHO multi-week window the WHO report accounts for every week. A non-WHO row that repeats the dashboard's value is a copy of it and is dropped; a source that reports a positive count in every week of the window shapes the WHO total in proportion to its counts (confidence 0.9; a curated shaped window keeps its curve); and every other non-WHO row in the window is then dropped, so a window never mixes the WHO total with another source's partial weeks. AI-extracted weeks that are aggregates mislabelled as a single week are dropped as well: an observed week of at least 20 cases that is at least five times every direct-source count within four weeks of it (Nigeria 2023 week 21, a year-to-date total), or that lies within 15% of a running total of the WHO weekly counts of its year (Congo 2023 week 29).

**Imputed weeks fill gaps only.** An imputed series spreads a total over every week of its span, and observed weeks that later replace part of that span are not netted out, so the imputed weeks that survive can repeat cases that observed weeks already report. In every country-year with a WHO account of the year (the annual total described under [Historical Incidence and Deaths](#historical-incidence-and-deaths), or else the year-to-date total of the WHO weekly rows), the imputed weeks may only fill the gap between that account and the observed and reconstructed cases: together they keep at most the difference, cases and deaths rescaled together, and a week rescaled below half a case is emptied. Documented absences of cholera, listed in the same curation table, empty the imputed weeks they contain (South Sudan from May 2023 to September 2024, Angola in 2023), and a contested imputed year is kept but listed in the adjustment log (Burkina Faso 2025).

**Downstream consumers.** Epidemic peaks (`est_epidemic_peaks()`) are detected on observed weeks only: imputed weeks are treated as missing, while a spread WHO report counts as observed because its total is reported. A detected peak whose window is at least half imputed is dropped, and documented outbreaks that the detector misses are added by hand. The training panel of the environmental suitability model (`compile_suitability_data()`) leaves a week without a case count missing, and the suitability model leaves such weeks out of its training targets. An optional interpolation of interior gaps of up to two weeks remains for the frozen legacy suitability model, which reads missing weeks as weeks without cases; it is off by default, because a filled week only adds an interpolated target, and a gap where no source reported cannot be told apart from one the reconciliation above emptied. Filled weeks are labelled `backfill_interpolated` and treated as imputed (tier 3): they carry a confidence weight of at most 0.5 and never set the scaling anchors of the suitability target. The calibration data leave those weeks missing.

## Vaccinations

Accurate data on oral cholera vaccine (OCV) campaigns and vaccination history are vital for understanding the impact of vaccination efforts. These data come from:

- **WHO Cholera Vaccine Dashboard**: This resource ([link](https://www.who.int/groups/icg/cholera)) provides detailed information on OCV distribution and vaccination campaigns from 2016 onward. Each extraction of the International Coordinating Group (ICG) request table is saved as a new dated snapshot (`who_vaccination_data_snapshot_<date>.csv`), written only when its content differs from the newest existing snapshot; earlier snapshots are never modified, and each new file is logged in the directory's provenance ledger (see *Provenance of raw data snapshots* below).
- **GTFCC OCV Dashboard**: Managed by Médecins Sans Frontières (Epicentre), this dashboard ([link](https://apps.epicentre-msf.org/public/app/gtfcc)) tracks OCV requests globally. Its event log, scraped by the `ees-cholera-mapping` pipeline (`cholera_vacc_requests.csv`), runs from 1 July 2013 to 16 December 2025 (deliveries to the 40 MOSAIC countries from 1 July 2014) and records, for each request, the request and the decision, every delivery (date, doses and vaccine product) and every campaign round (`C<campaign>-R<round>`, with the doses administered where reported). The letter in the request identifier gives the mechanism: `I` for a reactive request to the ICG and `G` for a preventive request to the GTFCC (four 2014 requests to MOSAIC countries carry an `L`).

We combine the two records with `combine_vaccination_data()`. A GTFCC row is one request, with its deliveries summed, and a WHO row is one shipment; a WHO shipment that matches a GTFCC request (by country, date and doses, or by ICG request number) is not counted again, and the combined record holds 182.8 million doses shipped to the 40 countries. The two kinds of GTFCC event play different roles. *Delivery* events drive the release of doses: `est_vaccination_rate()` releases each delivery on its own date into a stock administered at up to 20,000 doses a day. *Round* events drive the split into first and second doses: a request's shipped doses are divided across its rounds in proportion to the doses administered in each, and a round with an unreported dose count carries the request's mean reported round (see [Estimating vaccination rates](https://www.mosaicmod.org/model-description.html#estimating-vaccination-rates) on the Model Description page). Doses without round information count as first doses, and so do WHO-only rows, which carry no rounds. Three caveats apply:

- The processed files label every GTFCC row `context = "Outbreak response"`, because the log has no such field, so the label does not separate preventive requests from reactive ones; only the identifier does. In 2018--2022, 17 preventive requests carry 36.1 million of the 84.0 million doses released to the 40 countries.
- The one WHO-only shipment left (Malawi, 500,600 doses, April 2018, ICG request 20182) may repeat one of the two 500,600-dose deliveries of the GTFCC preventive request 2017-G03 to Malawi in March and May 2018, which the request-level match cannot pair.
- Two deliveries of exactly 664,400 doses to Malawi under the same programme, on 28 February 2020 (request 2017-G03-D01, completing its approval of 3.2 million doses) and on 6 November 2020 (request 2017-G03-D02, under its own approval of 676,000 doses), look like one shipment listed twice but belong to different approvals, and both are kept.

## Human Mobility Data

Human mobility patterns significantly influence cholera transmission. Relevant data include:

- **OAG Passenger Booking Data**: This dataset ([link](https://www.oag.com/passenger-booking-data)) offers insights into air passenger movements, which can be used to model the spread of cholera across regions.
- **Namibia Call Data Records**: An additional source from Giles et al. (2020) ([link](https://www.pnas.org/content/117/36/22572)) provides detailed mobility data based on mobile phone records, useful for localized modeling.

## Climate Data

Climate conditions, including temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, and extreme weather events, play a critical role in cholera dynamics. We assemble climate inputs from two upstream pipelines that we maintain alongside MOSAIC:

- **[open-meteo-pipeline](https://github.com/InstituteforDiseaseModeling/open-meteo-pipeline)**: a production pipeline that pulls daily-resolution variables from the [OpenMeteo Historical Weather Data API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) and the [OpenMeteo Climate Change API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/climate-api) for 30 uniformly distributed points within each MOSAIC country, splices ERA5 reanalysis with [MRI-AGCM3-2-S](https://www.wdc-climate.de/ui/cmip6?input=CMIP6.HighResMIP.MRI.MRI-AGCM3-2-S.highresSST-present) projections, spatially averages to the country level, and writes daily and weekly parquet files. MOSAIC reads these via `process_open_meteo_data()`. Variables include 2 m air temperature, dew point, relative humidity, 10 m wind, mean sea level pressure, cloud cover, shortwave radiation, precipitation, soil moisture at 0–7 cm (loaded as `soil_moisture_0_to_10cm_mean` for backward compatibility with the LSTM training data), and FAO evapotranspiration.
- **[enso-data](https://github.com/InstituteforDiseaseModeling/enso-data)**: a compiled time-series of the Indian Ocean Dipole Mode Index (DMI) and the Niño3, Niño3.4, and Niño4 indices of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), combining historical observations from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration ([NOAA](https://psl.noaa.gov/enso/)) with operational forecasts from NOAA's North American Multi-Model Ensemble ([NMME](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/NMME/), the default forecast source; the Australian Bureau of Meteorology [BOM](http://www.bom.gov.au/climate/ocean/outlooks/) feed remains available as a legacy alternative). MOSAIC reads these via `process_enso_data()`. The ENSO and DMI indices provide leading signals for environmental suitability over a ~9-month forecast horizon (NMME ENSMEAN).

Together these two pipelines supply the inputs of the 38 covariates (feature set `v7.3`) used by the LSTM model for environmental suitability $\psi_{jt}$: 16 local climate and 12 ENSO covariates directly, and 8 flood covariates through a model fitted to the EM-DAT flood records described below; the other two are seasonal cosines of the week of the year (see the [Model Description](https://www.mosaicmod.org/model-description.html#modeling-environmental-suitability) page).

### Storms and Floods

Data on extreme weather events, specifically storms and floods, are obtained from:

- **EM-DAT International Disaster Database**: Maintained by the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED) at UCLouvain, this database ([link](https://www.emdat.be/)) provides comprehensive records of disasters from 2000 to the present, including those affecting African countries.

### Drought

EM-DAT drought records are too long-lasting to serve as a weekly signal, so we derive a weekly drought label from each country's approximate standardised precipitation-evapotranspiration index: a country-week is drought-active when the 12-week rolling mean of the index is at or below $-0.8$. A binomial GAM (`impute_drought_probability()`) maps ENSO (Niño3.4) and Indian Ocean Dipole indices at lags of 8, 16 and 24 weeks, together with *antecedent* temperature and precipitation anomalies and accumulated precipitation, onto this label and predicts a drought probability for every country-week, historical and forecast. To avoid leakage, the concurrent index that defines the label is never a predictor, and every local-climate predictor is lagged by the 12-week label window so that it describes conditions strictly before that window. The GAM is fitted only on rows up to the observed-climate horizon -- the earlier of the last observed ENSO/IOD value and each country's last ERA5 reanalysis date -- so forecast-period climate never enters the fit; rows after the horizon are predicted, not fitted.

### Displacement

Internal displacement events are taken from the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre's Internal Displacement Updates ([IDMC](https://www.internal-displacement.org/)), downloaded as dated snapshots of the per-country mirrors on the [Humanitarian Data Exchange](https://data.humdata.org/) (38 of the 40 MOSAIC countries have a dataset) and expanded into weekly country panels of conflict- and disaster-driven displacement. Only records with the role *Recommended figure* are used: IDMC publishes each displacement once as a recommended figure, and the additional triangulation rows describe the same displacement, so summing both would double-count it (IDMC's own totals use recommended figures only).

## WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene)

Data on water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) are critical for understanding the environmental and infrastructural factors that influence cholera transmission. These data are sourced from:

- **WHO UNICEF Joint Monitoring Program (JMP) Database**: This resource ([link](https://washdata.org/data/household)) offers detailed information on household-level access to clean water and sanitation, which is integral to cholera prevention efforts.

## Demographics

Demographic data, including population size, birth rates, and death rates, are foundational for accurate disease modeling. These data are sourced from:

- **UN World Population Prospects 2024**: This database ([link](https://population.un.org/wpp/Download/)) provides probabilistic projections of key demographic metrics, essential for estimating population-level impacts of cholera.

## Provenance of raw data snapshots

Raw inputs that MOSAIC downloads automatically (EM-DAT, IDMC, World Bank, UN World Population Prospects, the mobility origin-destination sources, the travel-time friction raster, the WHO annual cholera record and the WHO ICG vaccination table) are written to the raw data directory as dated snapshots that are never overwritten. Each download goes to a temporary file, is validated, and is then moved into place, so an interrupted fetch cannot become the newest and therefore canonical file (the IDMC and mobility readers also skip an incomplete newer snapshot). Every new snapshot appends a row to a provenance ledger (`PROVENANCE.md`) in its source directory, recording when, from where and by which function it was obtained. All other raw files are hand-curated and read-only.
